North Carolina makers maintained a small-scale hand-crafted pottery tradition through the centuries, even as the craft became more industrialized throughout the rest of the United States. Copus attributed the rurality of the mountainous region as one factor that helped maintain the craft. Family heritage is another.
“There’s a phrase that gets used, which is ‘mud in the blood.’ It was such a part of people’s identity that they found ways to make it relevant,” Copus said.
Three Dimensional Tetris
The potters fired the kiln for three days. But it took Copus and his team several weeks of preparation before the fire could be lit. They acquired, sorted, and stacked several cords of wood, and mixed batches of wadding – a mixture of fireclay, sand, and sawdust that is used to keep pots from sticking during the firing. The hundreds of pieces of pottery, which had been made by the participants over the course of months, were decorated with slips and glazes, and then mounted on the thousands of clay and alumina wads.
Only then could the potters begin loading the kiln, which has approximately 300 cubic feet of stacking space divided into three different chambers.

“It’s a meticulous process. We’re setting the pieces in the kiln on shelves, so it’s like a big jigsaw puzzle or Tetris game,” Copus said. “I love the loading, I love the game of it, but it’s always a big relief when it’s done.”
The choices made while loading the kiln determined the path of the flame as it raced around the chambers, and the resulting surfaces of the pots. A lapse in concentration while loading the kiln could result in pieces sticking together or toppling over during the firing, ruining them.
“It’s been three non-stop days, from 10 am until dark, getting this kiln ready to go,” said Barao. “And that’s just the beginning.”
Once the kiln was loaded, the potters bricked up the doors and started a small campfire, which would eventually grow to fill all three chambers of the kiln. The potters divided themselves into three teams, which would tend to the fire around the clock in eight-hour shifts for the next three days.
“The early shifts are fairly relaxed. But as the firing progresses, the amount of wood and the rate at which we are adding it to the kiln increases. So by the end, you’re really doing like an arm-load of wood every three to five minutes for eight hours,” Copus explained.
The Flames Went Higher
Individual potters can easily fire gas and electric kilns independently. But wood-firing “is a team sport,” according to Copus. This is one of the elements that drew potters to travel from as far as Oklahoma and Ohio to participate in the firing.
“The part that I love most about wood firing is the communal nature, the community aspect of working together towards a common goal,” said Barao. “You can’t do it alone.”

Around half of the work in the kiln was Copus’. The remaining space was divided evenly among the other potters, who exchanged their labor for space in the kiln. But their collaboration went beyond merely getting the job done.
As Copus put it, “wood firing is hard, so why not make it fun?”
On the first night of the firing, community members and Copus’ friends and neighbors joined the potters for a pizza party (cooked, appropriately, in a wood-fired oven). Dinner was followed by ‘kilneoke’, an opportunity for the potters to serenade the kiln with songs about fire (including Johnny Cash’s ‘Ring of Fire’ and Sean Paul’s ‘Temperature’) and transformation (Joni Mitchell’s ‘Circle Game’, Van Morrison’s ‘Into the Mystic’).
Henry Crissman, who runs a community studio in Hamtramck, Michigan with his wife, Virginia Torrence, led the festivities. Crissman’s interest in wood firing is as sociological as it is artistic.
“The process is an instigator for this collective social experience,” Crissman said. “Wood firing could just be a tool and this could just be a factory where we’re making objects. But I think it’s pretty clearly not just that.”

That’s not to say that the visual results of the firing isn’t crucial for the participants. The other thing that keeps wood-firers coming back is the unique and unpredictable finish of the pottery.
“In wood firing, the spectrum is very wide, from complete and utter disappointment to total elation,” Copus said. “One of the things I love about it is that it can surprise you. You can actually make things that are beyond what you can imagine.”
The multi-day process of wood firing creates results that are unlike any other firing process. Gas, and especially electric firings, are largely predictable – you get out of it what you put into it. But as flames swirl through a wood kiln, they seek out oxygen in the clay, slips, and glazes – creating distinctive marks on the surfaces of the pots. Melted ash also glazes the pots in uncontrollable spurts, adding a shining layer to the ceramics.
“I’ve pulled things out of the kiln that I don’t even understand,” Copus said. “It’s alchemy, it’s magic.”
Copus emphasized that he and his team leave as little up to chance as possible – everything from the arrangement of the pots to the placement of the wood in the kiln is intentional. But wood firing is ultimately an uncontrollable process.
“It’s like the object becomes a record of the atmosphere that was moving around it,” Crissman explained. “And it’s exciting in the end when the object has some surface that is indicative of this story. Because we’ve had this experience together and in some way it’s recorded on the pot.”
Passing the Torch
Joseph Clayton and Ayden Krzmarzick drove 14 hours from Sand Springs, Oklahoma, to participate in the firing. Copus offered the two twenty-year-old potters a spot on the crew and a place to stay despite never having met them before. Mentoring younger potters is a responsibility Copus takes seriously – though he earned a BFA from the University of North Carolina, Asheville, his first introduction to ceramics was through a friend and mentor, Tom Phelps, when he was a teenager.
“I had so many great makers and mentors that took me under their wing and took the time to show me how to do stuff,” Copus said. “That’s what I try to do every day is pay that forward.”
The value of learning from more experienced potters is not lost on Clayton, who has also participated in wood firings in Denmark and France and is now working with Krzmarzick on building a wood fire kiln in their own community studio.
“It’s cool they’re continuing the cycle, and giving it to the next generation just like a million other potters have done before,” Clayton said. “Without the older generation showing the younger generation, none of this would be possible. So I think it’s really interesting to attempt to carry on the torch as best I can.”
“Nostalgia is a trap, really. Traditions need to evolve or they die. And so I think that’s a big part of what we’re trying to do here, is build on our traditions and keep it relevant to the contemporary world,” Copus said. “And so how do you do that? That’s what we’re trying to figure out.”

And they were salt glazing in Seagrove “Jugtown,” NC. [...] In NC, we have really educated buyers and they really appreciate pottery. So the first chamber is alot like their first chamber, just a lot bigger.

19 Mar Woodfire XIII with Rob Withrow
Rob unbricks the kiln.
Rob unbricks the kiln.
It’s like Christmas Eve over at Smoke in the Mountains Pottery today because it’s the day before the big wood kiln will be opened and unloaded. Many potters from all over the region contribute pots to be fired the traditional way in Rob Withrow’s huge wood kiln. This is Rob’s 13th wood firing at his studio. I stopped by and caught him taking a little peek inside the chamber and took the opportunity to talk to him about the firing and clay in general. Join us in the sneak peek…
CP: So what are you doing right now?
RW: I’m unbricking this kiln here that’s been cooling for five days. We heated it up to 2500 degrees using only wood, and now it’s like Christmas! You open it up and see what’s inside and this time the kiln fired so beautifully; it’s such a joy.
CP: Nice, How many time have you fired this kiln?
RW: It’s been a hard road but I stuck with it, and by golly the community came forth and helped me all along the way. I fired it nine times unsuccessfully. A weaker man would have caved or a smarter man would have stopped, but I kept going and here we are! The community came together and knew I was having problems. We put a new chimney on it and it works like a charm now. Now it’s a third of the wood, and a third of the time (than when we first started).
Beautiful pots from the March 2015 wood firing
Beautiful pots from the March 2015 wood firing
CP: How many times have you successfully fired it?
RW: This is number thirteen I am unloading, so four times without a hitch. The first nine times I had to unload it and re-fire everything. It was emotionally and financially draining. All the trial and error was worth it though. Now you look in here and the pots are just beautiful–they’re glowing! It’s just what I dreamed!
Not quite a 6-footer, but still a Large Face Jug by Rob Withrow, Wood Fired at Smoke in the Mountains, March 2015.
Not quite a 6-footer, but still a Large Face Jug by Rob Withrow, Wood Fired at Smoke in the Mountains, March 2015.
CP: You are known for throwing really tall face jugs. Do you have one in this firing?
RW: My passion is 6ft. pots. With the wood kiln, I can roll a 6 ft pot right in the chamber. This time it just fell over! I got the handle on it, signed it, it had an iguana on the top, and it just fell like a tree (laughs) you gotta be ready for that. That’s gonna happen every once in a while, if it was easy everyone would be doing it. You try to figure out why it happened and you just gotta know the next one will be better. There’s a lot of “ups”and “downs” in this business, but the “ups” are really up.
CP: Who was involved in this wood firing?
RW: Many different potters load pots and help with the firing. These folks had pots this time around: Harry and Julie B. Hearne (Turning Point Clay Studio, Brasstown, NC), Ted Cooley and Hannah Levin Cooley (Winding Stream Studio, Brasstown, NC), Chris Jones (Murphy, NC), Walter Aberson and Joyce Branch (Concord, NC), Evan Allhands (The Allhands Pottery, Cinncinatti OH) Maya Hamilton (Heritage Vision Creations, Brasstown, NC), Dick Aunspaugh (Young Harris, GA), and Ian my current apprentice who is completing a High School exit project.
Piggy Bank by Rob Withrow, Wood Fired at Smoke in the Mountains.
Piggy Bank by Rob Withrow, Wood Fired at Smoke in the Mountains.
The kiln is loaded with glazed pots.
The kiln is loaded with glazed pots.
CP: How many pots are in here?
RW: About 700 pots. Some are this big (points to a tiny thimble size bowl) and some are this big (points to his big pig bank).
I am really pleased. Everything I am seeing right now looks really good. Everyone worked so hard. We all take shifts and put wood in every 3-5 minutes for 28 hours. The new chimney is remarkable and has really cut down on the firing time.
My pots from this firing are headed to north of Chicago where I am going to have a show and a workshop hosted by Jill Tortorella of Antioch Pottery.
(Clink)
RW: Did you hear that? A pot just broke.
CP: Is that because you opened the bricks?
RW: Well it’s cool in here, so I’m not sure why that happened. That was a pot breaking though (laughs). Some of these are re-fired, so that might have something to do with it.
Rob fires the kiln. This wood firing took 28 hour, loading wood every 3-5 minutes!
Rob fires the kiln. This wood firing took 28 hour, loading wood every 3-5 minutes!
CP: So wood kilns are the traditional way of firing, right? And the NC has a rich pottery tradition? Can you talk about this?
RW: Yep, North Carolina does indeed have a rich history in pottery. From the 1700s we’ve be high firing pottery in NC. The Germans and the Irish brought the technology over with them. And they were salt glazing in Seagrove “Jugtown,” NC.
They had a traditional kiln called a “groundhog kiln.” I think the potters must have been bald, so they looked like little ground hogs coming out (laughs). This type of kiln is partly buried and has a real low arch, so you put your big pots in the middle and your smaller pots out to the side. It doesn’t have any shelves on it and it just sits on old flint and sand.
Burlon Craig was North Carolina’s last remaining Folk Potter doing things the traditional way. He would make his own glaze. To tell the temperature, he would let some glaze dry out and make a cone out of it. We he fired, he would watch the cone and know when it was done. They would also hook a pot and pull it out and look at it. That pot would be ruined but they’d know how the glaze was doing.
In NC, we have really educated buyers and they really appreciate pottery. Also in North Georgia, South Carolina and into Texas there is a wide band of natural clay, so that is where big pottery centers were located.

The community helps to unload the kiln, fire brigade-style.
CP: What inspired you to build a wood kiln?
RW: I learned most of my trade at the Folk School. I did a wood firing class at the Folk School with Ben Owens III and Charlie Liddell and then I just got hooked. The first time I saw the pots come out I knew that’s what I want to do. I fashioned this kiln after the Folk School kiln, I just super-sized it. So the first chamber is alot like their first chamber, just a lot bigger.
It’s a lot of work, but the results are just so beautiful that its worth all the labor. Every bowl and every mug has to be raised up off the shelf and sit on on little clay balls to keep it up so the ash from the burning wood doesn’t melt and weld it to the shelf. It’s a lot of labor. But it’s a sweet looking kiln. I look in there and it is just beautiful. And the back chamber will be even prettier because it got hotter.
This is a dream come true. I learned my whole trade at the Folk School. You could learn so many different trades there and now I get to go back and teach. I will be there till midnight many times because someone did that for me.
Large Face Jug with Snake by Rob Withrow, Wood Fired at Smoke in the Mountains.
Large Face Jug with Snake by Rob Withrow, Wood Fired at Smoke in the Mountains.
CP: How was your recent class?
RW: Oh we had a wonderful class! We had 11 students and Darrell Adams came and his grandpa was Bill Gordy a famous Folk Potter. I just love Darrell and it’s a pleasure to hand out with him for a week, He’s just a world of knowledge. He brings his ball mill and makes glaze out of rock. It was just a great firing we had. Evan Allhands was in that class and then we came over here and we loaded this one. I’m already excited to fire up the next one. I just cna’t get enough of it.
CP: Why so you like face jugs so much?
RW:  Well everyone’s done faces. Every culture that’s ever done clay has done faces. Your just looking at them all the time, so you are bound to put one on your pot. Our tradition here in the South started with slave potters. Some potters thought that the face on the jug kept the kids out of the moonshine, but I know that would be the first jug I’d go to if it had a face on it. So I don’t think that’s true.
I just love faces and now I’m doing these face mug parties. I just had 24 kids over here this morning, from Brevard. I make a blank mug on the wheel and then I show them how I put a face on. No one ever listens to me though because they are all different (laughs). And they’re all just so cool. They did great work.
Rob's happy with his pots from WFXIII!
Rob’s happy with his pots from WFXIII!
It’s amazing what people will do when you put clay in their hands. I think people are deprived of creativity and are deprived of touching the earth. I think that’s what’s gassing them. I just make it happen… getting people in the clay. It’s amazing what they come up with.
CP: Do you have any advice to aspiring potters?
RW: Make a lot of pots, that’s always been my theory! You are gonna make a thousand of crappy pots, so the sooner you get past them, the better off you are going to be. The more you deal with clay, the better you are going to get. I’ve been at it for 18 years and I’ll always be a student of clay. I just keep improving every year. It’s a lot of work and you have to be a self-starter, but I wouldn’t trade it for anything. I wake up everyday with a smile on my face and that’s straight from the heart.

Features & Essays
Kilns That Build Community
It takes a lot of work to fire up a kiln and keep it stoked. So artists often invite others to join in—helping both craft and community to flourish.
By Claire Voon  
November 14, 2022
Fall 2022
Ceramics
Free To Read

Photo by Conrad Calimpong
One of Conrad Calimpong's Ferndale, California, kilns fully stacked with ceramics from multiple artists participating in the firing.
Jasmine Oakley received the invitation in 2017: Come to California and help build a wood-fired kiln. For Oakley, then a sophomore at Eckerd College in Florida, traveling across the country to rural Mendocino County to lay bricks with strangers was a no-brainer. She had just built and fired a wood kiln at Eckerd for the first time under the guidance of ceramists Nick Schwartz and Brian Ransom, and was instantly hooked by the multi- day process. Schwartz and his wife, artist Jessica Thompson, were planning on doing it all over again that summer at the educational residency program they were hosting.
“Off the bat, they were doing a wood-firing—all these people I didn’t know, from many different backgrounds, from North Carolina, Japan, India,” Oakley recalls. “I was only 19, and I’m learning tips from people twice my age.” The group built another kiln, and the next year, Schwartz and Thompson invited Oakley back. She spent another idyllic summer by the fire, sharing meals with other artists, picking fruit, and cooling off by the river.
“Those two summers changed my whole life,” she says. “Before firing with Nick, I didn’t know who I was or what I wanted. When we’re wood-firing, we have our purpose. It doesn’t matter where you come from, what you do. All of that goes away, and you need to watch this fire.”
Jasmine Oakley and other students watch the final stoke of a seven-day anagama firing
Photo by Jasmine Oakley
Jasmine Oakley and other students witness the final stoke of a seven-day anagama firing in 2018 at Eckerd College in St. Petersburg, Florida.
Advertisement

“Deep friendships have been formed around the kiln and, in fact, a couple marriages. It teaches people how to communicate, how to solve problems together, conflict resolution.”
— Nick Schwartz
Tradition Revived
People have gathered around flames for millennia to fire ceramics with wood, watching as heat and ash mingle to leave singular marks on wares—glazes that are wholly natural. Originating in Southeast Asia and East Asia, the ancient tradition has survived despite the invention of gas and electric kilns. In recent years, it has even flourished. “The proliferation of wood kilns is so different from when I started in 1985—there were hardly any,” says Conrad Calimpong, who has kilns in Ferndale, California. “And now there’s hundreds.”
There are no official statistics on the number of wood kilns in the United States, but Illinois-based potter Simon Levin has been crowdsourcing a searchable map of them that illustrates their vast geographic spread (see simonlevin.com/map). Some are owned by schools and open mostly to students; others, like East Creek Anagama in Oregon, are community-based and host public workshops. Many are privately owned and were built to fire one artist’s ceramics.
The job, however, cannot be done solo. Kilns must be fired nonstop for days, sometimes for more than one week, requiring constant vigilance as flames dance around the wares. A rotating crew of stokers works in shifts that may last as long as 8, even 12, hours. Many kiln owners, like Schwartz and Thompson who now run Cider Creek Collective, invite artists to share kiln space in exchange for their labor; some also rent out space to cover material costs. Naturally, many kilns have evolved into community hubs, drawing regulars who reunite by the mesmerizing blaze.
“Deep friendships have been formed around the kiln and, in fact, a couple marriages,” says Schwartz, who has led community firings for three decades. “It teaches people how to communicate, how to solve problems together, conflict resolution.”
The process of wood-firing, from prep to cleanup, can take upwards of a month depending on the kiln type and size. There’s the noborigama, a traditional Japanese multi-chambered kiln for large-scale production that is designed to ascend a slope. One modern, time-saving option is the train kiln, whose structure recalls a locomotive and can be fired for one or two days. Perhaps the most popular structure is another traditional Japanese kiln, the anagama, an elongated dome–shaped furnace. “What sets it apart is that it takes full advantage of the wood-fire aesthetic because the fire is in direct contact with clay,” Schwartz says. “You get these massive ember beds that create an aesthetic you can’t really get any other way.”
Anandamayi Arnold and Nick Schwartz looking at a new pot from the anagama kiln.
Photo by Jess Thompson
Anandamayi Arnold (left) and Nick Schwartz looking at a new pot from the anagama kiln.
Around the Kiln, Around the Clock
The hard work of hardening clay begins long before a flame is lit. Firewood prep happens weeks, sometimes months, ahead, involving wood collection, then splitting pieces into manageable sizes. Next comes loading, a strategic operation that can take as long as two to four days and involve more than a thousand clay works. Ceramics nestle side by side, crammed onto shelves, every placement determining their final aesthetics. “The flame is like a glacial river, splitting, merging, and flowing, and you’re trying to create obstacles for the fire to change paths and go certain ways,” says Cynthia Morelli, who owns a kiln in Homer, Alaska. “You can work to get a load that enhances the works in the best possible way.”
Generally, greater color change happens as clay is increasingly exposed to heat. Encrusted patterns form as ash accumulates on surfaces, melts, and drips. Striking effects can transpire from the flashing of flames between pieces. Though the results are impossible to predict, stokers wield some degree of influence. They make adjustments depending on conditions such as temperature fluctuations, oxygen levels, how quickly wood is consumed, even the color of smoke. During a shift, one nurses the fire as frequently as every three to five minutes, aiming to hit certain temperature goals in different areas of the kiln.
“We’re trying to read the kiln constantly,” says Samuel Johnson, a professor at the College of Saint Benedict and Saint John’s University in central Minnesota, who built an anagama kiln on campus in 2012. “I listen constantly for the sound of combustion, for the sound of air moving through to the fire.”
When the flame is out—whether after 3 days or 10—the crew can recharge as the kiln cools. After about a week, the work recommences as they unload the goods, like archaeologists excavating treasures in an ancient, dusty chamber. This, too, must be done carefully to avoid breakage. (Although wadding, a refractory clay material, is placed around every piece during loading to prevent works from sticking, bonding still occurs. Separation may be achieved by sanding or grinding the pottery.) Finally, the crew cleans the kiln and polishes their creations.
The process is exhausting and at times brutal. To many wood-firers, it is also sacred, a kind of ritual steeped in history and tradition. Oftentimes, firings even begin with an offering to the kiln: flowers, or a splash of sake or whiskey into its mouth. “There’s a deep sense of camaraderie, but also respect for what’s going on—a kind of soberness,” Johnson says. “The firing cannot be ignored. There is a sense of, Okay, we’re in this together. And we’re going to do it in the middle of the night. We might be doing it during a blizzard. Or on 100-degree days. And if it’s hard, it doesn’t matter, because we’re going to be doing this.”
A loaded anagama kiln
Photo courtesy of Cynthia Morelli
Cynthia Morelli's Mamagama, a “tube-style” anagama kiln, loaded up at her studio in Homer, Alaska.
“Everything is dropped by the wayside while the firing is happening. I think that it really is a bonding experience for the people involved. It takes you to another place.”
— Cynthia Morelli
 A group of people dressed for a kiln firing in subzero temperatures.
Photo courtesy of Cynthia Morelli
Morelli (left) and resident artists Amanda Gentry, Heidi Kreitchet, and Zoë Powell, ready to start a November 2021 firing in subzero temperatures.
 Ceramic work by Morelli and Kreitchet after it was unloaded from the kiln.
Photo by Zoë Powell
Work by Morelli and Kreitchet after it was unloaded from the kiln.
Fêtes by the Fire
It helps that wood-firings are also fun. The occasion is not unlike a creative retreat or an art camp. As temperatures inside the kiln climb to more than 2000 ̊ F, artists may be hanging out nearby drinking tea, preparing meals together, or exchanging life stories. People may pitch tents on the grounds while others bunk in the host’s home. “Everything is dropped by the wayside while the firing is happening,” Morelli says. “I think that it really is a bonding experience for the people involved. It takes you to another place.”
In fact, no one really ever wants to leave the blaze, Oakley says, whether or not they are on a shift.“We find things to do around the kiln, and that’s our party. While people are loading or stoking, there’s this huge table where everyone brings dishes, and it’s a gathering of food and culture.”
Participants gather with food near Calimpong's kilns.
Photo by Conrad Calimpong
Participants gather with food near Calimpong's kilns.
“They’re surrounded with people who have dedicated their life to a world of aesthetics and art, and suddenly, it’s all within reach. They see these meaningful, deep life choices playing out.”
— Samuel Johnson
That mingling of perspectives is reflected inside the kiln, where pottery of all styles undergoes collective transformation. A single kiln may hold large urns, small bottles and bowls, and abstract clay shapes. Some may be glazed, though many artists prefer to embrace the natural glazing from ash, which can produce rich earth tones and an exquisite weathered look. Part of the intrigue is getting to see how other potters work and observe how a particular firing can influence one’s own practice. Artists surrender control to the process, allowing the elements to take charge. “I find it really liberating for a lot of people, especially artists who spend a lot of time in the studio,” Schwartz says. “They realize, Wow, there’s a creative dialogue happening, and all of a sudden my work is changing based on what I see other people doing and how they talk about their work.”
The experience can also be life-affirming as artists discuss their creative lifestyles. Johnson says such conversations are especially impactful for his students. “They’re surrounded with people who have dedicated their life to a world of aesthetics and art, and suddenly, it’s all within reach,” he says. “They see these meaningful, deep life choices playing out.”
Students look at their ceramic work after it's removed from the kiln.
Photo by Jasmine Oakley
Students in a Florida wood-fire kiln building class—run by Schwartz and Brian Ransom—look at their work after it’s removed from the kiln.
“...first-time firers use this experience as a jumping board. . . . You can create a network.”
— Conrad Calimpong
Destination Firings
The hugeness of undertaking a wood-firing limits how often they can happen. Artists cranking out pottery may follow a cycle as short as six to eight weeks, according to Schwartz, and hire stokers. But it’s also common for some to light their kilns just two or three times a year. Such wood-firings tend to be invitation-only or heard about through word of mouth (although many kiln owners also schedule firings with visiting artists that are open to anyone curious). Calimpong says he notifies friends months in advance of his interest in organizing firings at his Ferndale kiln, then works around their availability. Many attendees are regulars, including his first ceramics teacher, who has been showing up for a decade. Sometimes artists will bring friends, widening the circle of collaborators. They may have different skill levels and be guests at a kiln, but “we’re all on the same level, the same playing field,” Oakley says. “I’ve always felt comfortable at wood-fire gatherings.”
Potter Shumpei Yamaki, who fires his kiln near West Branch, Iowa, twice a year, operates with a democratic spirit. “I own a kiln, but it’s not just my kiln,” he says. “I don’t put my name first. I like to cultivate the idea of sharing. My philosophy is that a great community and a great team can produce better results because you can have a great vibe.” This shared time, he adds, ideally gives artists reason to return to his studio and develop more projects together, whether firings or an exhibition.
For young potters in particular, the experience can provide opportunities to learn from seasoned ceramists, lead to exhibitions, and increase access to other kilns. “A lot of students who are first-time firers use this experience as a jumping board. When they go to another kiln, if the person knows who I am, that kind of gives them a foot in the door,” Calimpong says. “You can create a network.”
Firing crew in front of a kiln
Photo by anonymous, courtesy of Shumpei Yamaki
Tab Link (left), Meg Billingham, Jess Lease, and Shumpei Yamaki in front of Yamaki's kiln at a 2021 firing.
Kilns tend to be in remote locations—there’s less chance, after all, of someone calling the fire department. Participants, therefore, often come from out of town, even outside the country. Calimpong has hosted people from as close as the San Francisco Bay Area to as far as Hungary and Germany. Artists often drive hours with their work or have pieces shipped, sometimes as bisqueware, which is fired at a lower temperature for durability.
Visiting different kilns takes commitment, but doing so enhances a potter’s perspective, as no two firings are the same. Plus, kilns produce varied effects depending on their architecture and firing team. “Each person fires a kiln very differently, so you get the beautiful opportunity to peer into someone’s insight, experience, and instinct,” Oakley says. “Each kiln has its own personality.”
Two years out of college, Oakley has built a half-dozen kilns since her first encounter with wood-firing. She is now designing her own to stand on her family’s land in Middlesex County, Virginia, using bricks made from local clay. Although she has been flying to Florida to lead firings at her alma mater, she wants to create something nearby that carries her own character—and a place where she can develop another legacy.
Wood-firing, she says, “led to me coming home to myself and my identity.” She wants to help other artists feel a similar sense of belonging. “Through wood-fire, you find your family, because you have people who understand you in a way that no one else does—the primitive side of you, the side that gets delirious because you’ve been up all night,” Oakley says. “It’s not just about putting a piece in the kiln. It’s like people are putting you back together. Your identity is reshaping because, finally, someone understands you in different ways. They see me.”
Claire Voon is a Brooklyn-based journalist and critic who has contributed to publications including theNew York Times, Artforum,and the Brooklyn Rail.
A batch of ceramics ready to be unloaded from a kiln.
Photo by Shumpei Yamaki
A batch of ceramics from a 2022 firing ready to be unloaded from Shumpei Yamaki's kiln in West Branch, Iowa.

Photo by Conrad Calimpong
A stack of wood ready for a firing at one of Conrad Calimpong's kilns in Ferndale California.

Wood Firing Fundamentals with Dakota Joan Parkinson
Wood Firing Workshop

“Groundhog” style wood/soda kiln
Cone 10
Load/Fire: August 29 – 31
Unload: September 5
Price: $160 registration, $40 material fee paid to instructor
This workshop will be centered in the fundamental firing techniques of our North Carolina style groundhog kiln and span three days of firing focused on natural ash surfaces and ember bed effects. My goals are not to teach you how to run the kiln exactly as I do, but to instead supply the tools to problem solve and work collaboratively in understanding how to bring any atmospheric kiln to temperature and seek the surfaces that bring you joy.
We will be focused on basic woodfiring principles, firing by audio and visual cues, monitoring and feeding the coal bed, how to load for dynamic surfaces, and adapting these practices to a kiln without sidestoking. We will be firing in a classic cone 10 to 13 temperature range with a hard shut down to encourage matte, ashy, and ember-rich surfaces. All styles of work have a place in this workshop, including sculptural and functional forms.
Each participant should bring approximately 6 cubic feet of cone 10 bisqueware. We encourage participants to bring more to allow us to fill the kiln more effectively, and to include as many additional 3x2x2 inch stuffer pieces as possible to fill gaps in the kiln.
My teaching approach is deeply collaborative. In this intimate setting you will have hands-on access to the kiln, will be leading shifts, and will receive direct guidance as you problem-solve alongside me. Space is limited, so you can expect plenty of time at the kiln and a close-knit community of makers working toward glowing ash surfaces and ember bed effects.
Day 1 – Students will arrive at the Morean Center for Clay at 9:30am, Dakota-Joan will give an artist talk and discuss with the group the overarching firing goals. We will spend the day discussing glazing and loading strategies as we load the kiln together. On this day we will set the firing schedule and shifts for the remaining workshop time.
Day 2/3 – Students will work together during their agreed upon shifts to fire the groundhog kiln. On these shifts they will learn the details of monitoring the kiln, managing the coal bed and wood stoking patterns. Dakota will be available for hands-on teaching at the beginning of most shifts for demonstration of safe practices and shift expectations. It is recommended that students are present for the final shift in order to learn about kiln shut down. Post shutdown, kiln will need to cool for several days. 
Day 4 – Unload ! Students arrive at the Morean at 10am, unload the kiln, take part in a retrospective discussion and clean the kiln. Additionally, Dakota-Joan will demonstrate her methods for cleaning and finishing the fired work. 

Learn more about Dakota here!
Dakota Joan is an educator, maker, and community builder. She believes in nontraditional paths into art and values wood-firing for its connection to labor and history—she cut her teeth firing wood kilns in Missouri as a studio assistant while also working as a microbiologist. She teaches workshops out of St. Petersburg, Florida, where she is a technician at the Morean Center for Clay and a studio manager at the Hive Community Clay.

AVL Clay - Asheville's Community Pottery Studio
AVL Clay is Asheville’s new membership-based community pottery studio, created to foster creativity, connection, and craftsmanship through clay. Located in a beautifully restored 1920s industrial building along the Swannanoa River, AVL Clay offers memberships, classes, workshops, and private events for artists of all skill levels — from first-time beginners to experienced ceramicists.
Founded by ceramic artist Arleen Ferrara in 2025, AVL Clay was born from a desire to rebuild creative space and community following the loss of many local studios after Hurricane Helene. The 4,300-square-foot studio features 12 pottery wheels, a slab roller, multiple kilns, 13 custom glazes, and a welcoming environment designed to inspire collaboration and artistic growth.
Members enjoy open studio access (9 AM–9 PM daily), personal storage, firing services, and a growing calendar of workshops and community programs.  
AVL Clay is open to all artists who believe in the power of creativity and connection.
Learn more or apply for membership at www.avlclay.com or follow @avl.clay on Instagram and Facebook.

Whether you’re stepping into your professional practice, craving community, or looking for a studio that helps you take your work to the next level, our Studios offer an inspiring, well-equipped home for serious ceramic artists.
What to expect when you join us!
Community Studio Access
Enjoy studio access seven (7) days a week (excluding holidays). Each tenant has a designated professional space with everything you need in house, including:
 A dedicated community glaze and work area (including access to the glaze kitchen)

Your studio is your own to set up with your tools/equipment, arrange your workflow, and develop your practice.

By maintaining a non-toxic studio environment, we protect the health and well-being of every artist and create a space where creativity can flourish safely.
Build Your Professional Presence
Become part of our welcoming, open, and vibrant creative community, recognized across Western North Carolina and beyond.  
As a tenant artist, you’ll gain more than studio space, you’ll become part of a supportive environment that values connection, creativity, and visibility:
 A credible and inspiring home base for your creative practice
 A place to welcome customers, collectors, and potential buyers
 Visibility within our nationally recognized ceramic center
Artists seeking to be represented in the gallery may also apply to display their work in our curated Fine Ceramic Arts Gallery, a year-round destination for collectors, students, and art enthusiasts.
Creative Community
Becoming a Working Studio tenant means joining a supportive network of artists who share knowledge, offer encouragement, and build one another up. You’ll be surrounded by fellow ceramicists who take their craft seriously and value the richness that comes from working in community.
Limited Availability
Our Working Studio community is intentionally small and highly sought after. Space is limited, availability changes throughout the year, and an application is required and we do keep a waitlist.

Our Community
Firefly Valley Design celebrates diversity, prioritizes equity, and lives out inclusion. This is the core of who we are as people and neighbors. We believe in the power of community when it comes together in authentic ways to share gifts and strengths. We aim to create and maintain an environment that is safe, nurturing, and fosters discovery for all gender identities, sexual orientations, ages, abilities, races, ethnicities, socioeconomic levels, and neurodiversity.
​
bipoc.png
Founder
Ona Armstrong  Founder and Lead Teacher
I was born a maker, in the mountains of Virginia. I was home-schooled until ten years old, running barefoot with a paintbrush in my hand. Raised by artists, musicians and craftspeople, my fondest memories from childhood were of raising goats, weaving, painting, making fairy houses. We built tree houses and played endlessly on our 30 acres outside of Lexington, VA. I was also a dancer from the age of four and continued to dance through high school, touring our area and performing with my troupe. I  attended Bennington College in Vermont as a Harcort Scholar, graduating with a degree in ceramics and education in 2000 and graduated again with a Masters of the Arts in Teaching from Bennington in 2003. 
​​
Arriving in Asheville in 2004, I began my teaching journey in Kindergarten at Evergreen Community Charter School. I loved teaching young children, intertwining movement and music with academic skills and social-emotional learning. While I was there, I was able to write plays, make large puppets, coordinate performances, play music, dance, and design a nature playscape. ​ In 2017, I left traditional teaching as I made the transition to business owner, exploring ways that I could apply my passion for facilitating my own and other's creativity and expression.   
​
As the founder of Firefly Valley Design and Consulting, I am a traveling arts consultant, offering arts for personal expression and interpersonal connection. As a teacher, I am warm and funny. I am prepared and professional, working in collaboration with program directors, therapists and families/corporations to arts accessible to everyone. I engage groups of people in artistic endeavors that allow for expression and connect them with each other. Arts for expression and connection is my life's calling. 
​
I am so excited to be on this journey with you.
The Firefly Valley Team
Get to know the amazing teachers who make up the Firefly Valley team.
Firefly Valley Staff
rachel-FV.jpg
Rachel Appleton     (she/they)
I first discovered my love of clay when I was a young child digging in the natural springs of Florida. My godmother taught me how to make a coil pot and we baked it over a bonfire. I cherish the piece that still sits on my mantle today.
In high school, I took pottery classes every semester and grew an appreciation for the history and science of clay. After graduating high school, I continued my education in pottery at ABTech Community College.
For over 10 years, I have taught people of all ages and abilities to connect with clay in a patient, grounded and playful way. 
Working with clay has been healing for my anxiety and grief as an adult and I am passionate about nurturing the creative and emotional parts of artists who sit with me at the wheel.
At Firefly Valley, I teach our Teen Pottery Class, Women’s Pottery Church, and Summer Camp. It is such an honor to be a part of the Firefly Valley community.
diedre-firefly-valley-pottery.jpg
Deidre Barrett     (she/they)
After being a happy elementary teacher in Asheville for decades, the freedom and creativity in Firefly Valley speaks to my heart & soul! I love my Summertime camp weeks of messy, muddy fun, of learning, growing, and creating with amazing colleagues and happy, laughing kiddos. I’m a sci-fi geek and arts & crafts buff. My hobbies include being a quintessientual cat lady, a bookworm, garden gnome and foodie.  I am a novice at pottery, but a very enthusiastic learner!
bermingham.jpeg
Gabriela Bermingham    (she/her)
My name is Gabriela Bermingham and I am a native Spanish speaker, born in Puerto Rico to Cuban parents.   
I have been a school teacher for 20+ years and of those years, I have been teaching Spanish to elementary aged students for 11 years. I am currently a Spanish teacher at IC Imagine Charter School teaching grades K-5.  
It is such a joy to be able to pass on the gift of language to other students. It brings me great happiness to teach Spanish to young learners and see their enthusiasm as they learn a new language while also learning about different Latin and Hispanic cultures. I am thrilled to be the Spanish teacher at Firefly Valley Pottery Camp this summer the week of June 15th! See you soon!
catina.png
Catina Clarice Briscoe     (she/her)
I am a throwing and hand building teacher at Firefly Valley camp and I’m really excited to be here.  
I’m a maker of beautiful things. I make functional pieces, as well as abstract items, using challenging techniques or more simple objects. I love them all.  
I enjoy playing with many mediums from clay to plants to whatever I can get my hands on, that speaks to me.    
I enjoy supporting others expressing themselves and come to know themselves, through their experiences with nature and creativity.
melissa-firefly-valley-pottery.jpg
Melissa Butler     (she/her)
This is my third year working at Firefly Valley Pottery, and I absolutely love it!  I am a retired special education teacher and a transplant from Texas.  I enjoy watching kids unplug and get outside.  I think it is important for children to tap into their creative side and realize there are not right and wrong answers when making art. I like to hike in the mountains, float on rivers, and watch a baseball game at McCormick field.
chad-firefly-valley-pottery.png
Chad Caldwell     (he/him)
Hi, I am a visual arts teacher for grades K-5 here Fairview Elementary School. I was born and raised in the beautiful Appalachian Mountains.  
I have been teaching art since 2012. I graduated from Western Carolina University with a BS. of Education in Art, a BS. of Education in Elementary Education, and a BFA in Photography. 
I love teaching art and I believe that art is an essential part of every child's overall education. Because I believe that the arts are interconnected to math, science, language arts, social studies, and basically all areas of study, I practice an integrative approach to teaching.
marissa-bio.jpg
Marissa Domanski   (she/her)
I grew up in the Green Mountains of Vermont and was lucky enough to live in Maui, HI for three years before finding my way to the Blue Ridge Mountains of WNC in 2008.  
I have been drawn to clay ever since my first pottery class in high school. From there, I went to Alfred University to continue my exploration of clay and have sought out workshops and teachers to help me develop my craft ever since.  
I now work out of my home studio in Weaverville. When I’m not making pots, I work as a bookkeeper for artists and creatives, and dance whenever I can! I loved being a part of the community here at Firefly Valley last year, and am looking forward to much more creativity, growth and fun this summer!
SHANE.jpg
Shane Donaldson   (he/him)
Shane Donaldson is a ceramic artist from Asheville, a father and instructor at Odyssey Clayworks in the River Arts District.
ms-susanne.jpg
Suzanne Junkin Friedrichs   (she/her)
I am a self-taught watercolor, pastel, and ceramic hand-building artist and teacher from Lexington, VA.
I taught K through 2nd grade classes in Fine Arts in Rockbridge County and at Earthsong Montessori School.  I enjoy teaching hand-building ceramics at Firefly Valley Pottery. I'm also Ms. Ona's mama! 
I like to stay busy with my own hand-building project of nature-themed plaques and miniature sculptures called Wild Solace, subbing with Firefly Valley Pottery children's classes, and playing my hammered dulcimer.
sara-goodwin.png
Sara Goodwin   (she/her)
I’m excited to join a community of creative, like‑minded educators and artists at Firefly Valley Pottery. I see pottery, gardening, and nature‑based learning as powerful ways to help young people root themselves in place and grow into thoughtful, grounded humans.
I am a horticulturist, herbalist, and lifelong student of the Appalachian ecosystem, with more than twenty years of experience studying the plants, soils, and cultural traditions of this region. I hold an MS in Agricultural Education from NC A&T and an AS in Horticulture Technology, and I ground my work in both scientific understanding and hands‑on land stewardship. As an herbalist trained through the Chestnut School of Herbal Medicine, I bring an understanding of native and medicinal plants and their uses. I am also a Certified Plant Professional with extensive plant identification knowledge and experience in ethical foraging.
​
For the past five years, I’ve served as a 5th grade associate at Evergreen Community Charter School, where I support inquiry‑based learning and help young people build confidence outdoors. 
My family and I live on a ten‑acre farm in West Asheville, where we raise animals, grow food and a diverse herb garden. As a child, I lived off‑grid in the woods of Maine, where I developed an understanding of seasonal rhythms, ecological interdependence, and the importance of passing this knowledge from one generation to the next. I am passionate about helping children experience nature in ways that cultivate curiosity, respect, and a sense of belonging.

John Quick at the wheel in the clay studio

John Quick at the wheel in the clay studio

Overview
The Penland clay studios support workshops in traditional and contemporary clay vessel making and sculpting. The studios are flexible, and are particularly well-equipped for throwing, handbuilding, moldmaking and casting using a range of clay bodies and firing options. Our programming is current in spirit and respectful of craft traditions. Workshops take place in two well-maintained studios designed to accommodate diverse content and working styles in a safe environment.
Studio & Classroom Space
The two studios, Upper Clay and Lower Clay, are slightly different, but both have a large, common work area with individual work stations and covered, outdoor work and leisure space. They share covered kiln sheds with electric, gas, salt, soda, raku, and wood kilns. Both studios also have smaller, attached rooms with large, shared tables for extra work space and for activities like glazing and mold making. Additionally, both studios have shared sinks and a computer workstation. In Upper Clay, there is a separate glaze mixing lab with dry ingredients and dedicated ventilation, which is shared between the two studios.
Both studios are accessible from the outside and there is an accessible parking space adjacent to the clay studios.
Student Workspace & Storage
There are up to 16 students in Upper Clay workshops and up to 15 in Lower Clay. Each student has an individual workspace, either a potter’s wheel and shelving unit or a work table with storage underneath, along with appropriate seating. Ware carts are used to store finished green and bisque ware before and between firings.
Tools & Materials
Students purchase clay from the studio – please do not bring any clay from home. This ensures there will be no surprises when we open the kiln.
The clay studio has some general clay working tools available for loan such as wire tools, throwing sponges, wooden tools, pin tools, wooden rib tools, ruler, compasses, and calipers, as well as plenty of towels, buckets, and aprons for student use. The Penland Supply Store carries a variety of clay tools for purchase. Students are encouraged to bring their own favorite clay tools, brushes, stamps, paddles, slip-trailers, sgraffito tools, sketchbooks, and drawing supplies.

Seagrove North Carolina clay studio kiln.snippet:
The workshop will explore a variety of functional and decorative styles, reflecting foundational elements of Ben’s family pottery traditions and his studies in college and abroad. Some forms will be constructed in multiple parts and assembled during the workshop. Attention will be given to finishing techniques, details, and various approaches to glazing and firing, with a focus on surface enhancement.
Ben will also share his philosophy and design process, offering insights into his specific methods of working with clay, as well as the rich pottery traditions of the historic Seagrove area in North Carolina. Participants will be encouraged to engage in open discussions throughout the workshop, fostering a collaborative and enriching learning environment. [...] The annual firing of the Peters Valley anagama, “Emily,” will be led by Ben Owen III for August 2022, located in Layton New Jersey. For the past 20 years, noted artists from around the world have led the firing, and this year we are honored to offer the opportunity to fire with Ben Owen III, from Seagrove, North Carolina. This firing promises to be a fascinating and special experience. Participants will bring bisque-fired HIGH temperature stoneware or porcelain works to be included in the kiln. Some slips and glazes will be available for participants to use before the loading. Techniques for loading the kiln will be covered, including the use of wadding, tumble-stacking, and positioning of the wares in order to promote the most dynamic flame marks. The firing requires at least five days [...] Ben Owen III is an American potter born and raised in Seagrove, North Carolina. A sixth-generation ceramist learning from his family, Owen holds a BFA in Ceramics at East Carolina University. He was awarded a fellowship in Japan, and was a visiting artist in Jingdezhen, China. Ben continues to work in the family business, “Ben Owen Pottery,” established by his grandfather and father. Wood firing has continued to influence Ben's work by creating moments in time for color and surface effects from the process.
For more information about this special workshop, visit the Sugar Maples Center for Creative Arts website.

Ben Owen III Workshop at the Bascom Art Center -Soda/Salt Kiln Firing & Wheel Throwing Workshop Summer 2025
 The Bascom Art Center (map)
 Google Calendar ICS
Workshop is Full
The workshop begins with glazing demonstrations and an exploration of options for enhancing effects in soda firing. Techniques such as the use of flashing slips for accents and brushwork will be introduced, alongside traditional glazes. Participants are asked to bring 10-20 small (4”-6”h) and medium (9”-12”h) pots. Plates are not recommended, though bowls with a diameter of up to 8” are acceptable. A variety of pieces is encouraged to maximize learning opportunities.
Once the soda kiln is loaded, it will be preheated overnight and fired to completion the following day. A discussion of the firing process will be integral, providing participants the chance to assist with kiln adjustments and the addition of soda during the final stages of firing. While the kiln is firing, participants will have time to begin creating pots on the wheel, focusing on techniques for shaping and altering clay.
The workshop will explore a variety of functional and decorative styles, reflecting foundational elements of Ben’s family pottery traditions and his studies in college and abroad. Some forms will be constructed in multiple parts and assembled during the workshop. Attention will be given to finishing techniques, details, and various approaches to glazing and firing, with a focus on surface enhancement.
Ben will also share his philosophy and design process, offering insights into his specific methods of working with clay, as well as the rich pottery traditions of the historic Seagrove area in North Carolina. Participants will be encouraged to engage in open discussions throughout the workshop, fostering a collaborative and enriching learning environment.
For more information on the workshop, visit the Bascom Art Center website.

Ben offers a special opportunity this summer in the Catskills of New York. This pivotal workshop will provide a great experience of wood-firing as a group. Participants will bring bisque ware to prepare for the firing. iVarious approaches to using flashing slips, glazing with materials to create texture, and firing techniques will be emphasized. Ben Owen III is an American potter born and raised in Seagrove, North Carolina. A sixth-generation ceramist learning from his family, Owen holds a BFA in Ceramics at East Carolina University. He was awarded a fellowship in Japan, and was a visiting artist in Jingdezhen, China. Ben continues to work in the family business, “Ben Owen Pottery,” established by his grandfather and father. Wood firing has continued to influence Ben's work by creating moments in time for color and surface effects from the process.

 Ben Owen Pottery (map)

The annual firing of the Peters Valley anagama, “Emily,” will be led by Ben Owen III for August 2022, located in Layton New Jersey. For the past 20 years, noted artists from around the world have led the firing, and this year we are honored to offer the opportunity to fire with Ben Owen III, from Seagrove, North Carolina. This firing promises to be a fascinating and special experience. Participants will bring bisque-fired HIGH temperature stoneware or porcelain works to be included in the kiln. Some slips and glazes will be available for participants to use before the loading. Techniques for loading the kiln will be covered, including the use of wadding, tumble-stacking, and positioning of the wares in order to promote the most dynamic flame marks. The firing requires at least five days and nights with emphasis placed on cooperation, collaboration. and working together to achieve a beautiful and successful result.
\ The unloading of the kiln will take place on Sunday, August 21st.
For more information about this special workshop, visit the Peters Valley website.

Taking place at Peter’s Valley Craft Center in Layton, New Jersey, this workshop is a unique opportunity to make your own work alongside one of the country’s preeminent potters. Participants will work at their own pace while at the same time be introduced to Owen’s ways of making work for an anagama kiln. Techniques such as sectional and coil throwing large forms will be shared. Also, ways of thinking about forms with regards to what happens to them during a long firing will be discussed. There will be a number of different clay bodies available, as well as several from Starworks [North Carolina] that the instructor will bring for participants to explore. Presentations and discussions will round-off the workshop with this special artist. Work produced in this workshop will be included in the firing of the anagama that follows. A Learn to Turn (L2T) workshop in progress.
LEARN TO TURN WORKSHOPS
Learn to Turn (L2T) workshops are designed forages 16 and older; no age exceptions.
No experience is required for L2T Beginner’s Turning Workshops.
L2T experience or equivalent required for L2T Intermediate/Advanced/Specialty Workshops.
L2T is a one-time beginner's pottery class great for individuals, families, friends, and dates. Get a feel for how clay moves on the wheel before investing in a series of continuing education classes or expensive studio equipment. Celebrate a birthday, anniversary, or other social occasion with the gift of a shared learning experience!
Clay, glaze, and kiln firings all included. Students receive a detailed throwing demonstration, before trying it out for themselves. Focus is on process not products. While learning to operate the equipment and access the studio space safely students will also gain firsthand knowledge of basic pottery-turning techniques.
Up to 90 minutes of class is used for practicing methods of centering, opening, and pulling up a cylinder. An experienced instructor will work with each student to prepare 1 pot on the wheel (up to 3 may be kept) that will be fired and can be picked up in about 4 weeks.
Group learning experiences are not equivalent to receiving private lessons, as each student may be in a different work stage, requiring alternating levels of attention throughout the event. Beginners are welcome to register for more L2T workshops to continue practicing their potter's wheel basic skills.
Private workshop requests can be emailed to education@ncpotterycenter.org.
PLEASE NOTE:
While photos are allowed, we do not allow participants to videotape or livestream workshops (public or private) for liability, privacy, and security reasons.
Our policies are subject to change.

John Quick at the wheel in the clay studio

John Quick at the wheel in the clay studio

Overview
The Penland clay studios support workshops in traditional and contemporary clay vessel making and sculpting. The studios are flexible, and are particularly well-equipped for throwing, handbuilding, moldmaking and casting using a range of clay bodies and firing options. Our programming is current in spirit and respectful of craft traditions. Workshops take place in two well-maintained studios designed to accommodate diverse content and working styles in a safe environment.
Studio & Classroom Space
The two studios, Upper Clay and Lower Clay, are slightly different, but both have a large, common work area with individual work stations and covered, outdoor work and leisure space. They share covered kiln sheds with electric, gas, salt, soda, raku, and wood kilns. Both studios also have smaller, attached rooms with large, shared tables for extra work space and for activities like glazing and mold making. Additionally, both studios have shared sinks and a computer workstation. In Upper Clay, there is a separate glaze mixing lab with dry ingredients and dedicated ventilation, which is shared between the two studios.
Both studios are accessible from the outside and there is an accessible parking space adjacent to the clay studios.
Student Workspace & Storage
There are up to 16 students in Upper Clay workshops and up to 15 in Lower Clay. Each student has an individual workspace, either a potter’s wheel and shelving unit or a work table with storage underneath, along with appropriate seating. Ware carts are used to store finished green and bisque ware before and between firings.
Tools & Materials
Students purchase clay from the studio – please do not bring any clay from home. This ensures there will be no surprises when we open the kiln.
The clay studio has some general clay working tools available for loan such as wire tools, throwing sponges, wooden tools, pin tools, wooden rib tools, ruler, compasses, and calipers, as well as plenty of towels, buckets, and aprons for student use. The Penland Supply Store carries a variety of clay tools for purchase. Students are encouraged to bring their own favorite clay tools, brushes, stamps, paddles, slip-trailers, sgraffito tools, sketchbooks, and drawing supplies.

Each Spring and Fall, Rising Sun Pottery hosts a Saturday raku firing. All students and area potters are invited. Everyone brings pots and if there are enough potters attending, we have a pot luck lunch with Rising Sun providing the burgers and drinks. Otherwise, we "pizza" in! Fun is had by all as we make a day of raku, good food, and socializing. Our Spring Raku Saturday will be held on Saturday, May 23, 2020, and the Fall Raku Saturday is scheduled for Saturday, October 24, 2020. Both events start at 11 AM. Everyone is invited, so start making pots now for a day of fun, fire and smoke.

Wildacres Retreat Conference Center Workshops
The July 4th week pottery retreat is held at Wildacres Retreat Conference Center, located in Little Switzerland, NC, just off the Blue Ridge Parkway. This workshop is a pottery retreat for
learning and socializing with other potters and making great pots. The studio is open 24 hours
Rising Sun provides a guest pottery instructor, and workshop leader Gary Lee is available to work with anyone who may want additional instruction. Gas cone 10, sagger and raku firings are available during the week. The workshop fee includes meals, lodging, firing fees, and instruction fees. The 2019 retreat was a great success with Sylvia Coppola of Duck Creek Pottery, Indian Trail, NC, as our guest instructor. There were cone 10 gas firings and several days of raku, sagger and horsehair firings. The workshop results were beautiful, presenter Sylvia Coppola wonderful, the margaritas cold, the weather was great and the location was out of this world!
For 2020, our 23rd Annual Summer "it was a dark and stormy night pottery guild" workshop will be held Sunday June 28 through Saturday, July 4, 2020. Cost is $480.00 and includes lodging, meals, and all fees. For 2020 our guest instructor will be an encore presentation by Sylvia Coppola. Call or e-mail for space availability.
The September workshop is a true retreat for potters who are looking for a week away from the everyday distractions at home. Gary offers instruction to improve on any techniques you may have problems with and for you to learn new methods in throwing. Or, if you are just looking for a workshop to "throw your life away" for a week in the beautiful setting of the North Carolina mountains, this is your chance. There will be gas cone 10 and raku and firings available during the week along with instruction on how to fire these kilns.
Our 2020 9th Annual Fall meeting of the "it was a dark & stormy night pottery guild" will be held Monday, August 24 through Sunday, August 30, 2020. Cost is $465.00 which includes meals, lodging, firing fees and instruction. Call or e-mail for space availability. This workshop is limited to 14 attendees.
Rising Sun Pottery also helps organize potters who wish to attend the Wildacres Retreat Conference Center annual Spring and Fall Artist Gatherings. In addition, Gary manages the studio during this week, so if you need help with anything, it is available. There are cone 10 gas firings, sagger, and Raku firing during the week. This event gives potters the experience of socializing with artists from other media fields: painters, jewelry makers, nature printers, and writers to name a few. The 2020 Spring Artist Gathering at Wildacres Retreat and the Fall Artist Gathering dates have not been announced yet. Go to Wildacres.org for 2020 event dates, application schedules, payment deadlines and costs, which include lodging (double occupancy), meals, gratuities, firing fees and other mountaintop activities during the week. Please do not send checks before application windows opens. All artists of any medium are welcome. Space is limited in the Pottery studio.

Wildacres is on top of a mountain, so there is nothing to do except what you are there for. No TV, radio, newspapers and sparse cell phone coverage minimize distractions. If you wish, take a half-day "road trip" to a local pottery studio or visit Penland Craft School, which is only 30 minutes away.
Make "BIG" pots
Every few years we have a "BIG" pots workshop, a two-day challenge to
make big pots from thrown sections. Check back for the date and time for
the next "BIG" pots workshop.
Spring Mug Sale - Mugathon
For those of you who are not aware, we have temporary postponed our
annual Mug for Mutts and Cups for Cats Benefit indefinitely. However, we
will be continuing our support of the Humane Society of Lincoln County
by making a yearly donation equal to what we raised in 2018 at our 21st
Annual event. Hopefully we will be able to restart this event in the coming years.
Thank you for your support over the years. The Cats and Dogs very much appreciated
your support.
Fall Empty Bowl Soup Benefit
The 23rd Annual Empty Bowl benefit for Hospice Palliative Care of Lincoln County will
be held Tuesday, October 13, 2020 at 5 p.m. Our 22nd Annual Benefit held in October
2019 was an overwhelming success. We sold out of 337 bowls and took prepaid orders
for 30 more bowls! What a great outpouring of support from our community for Hospice in Lincoln County. The bowls are made by RSP students and instructors. Rising Sun volunteers make the wonderful Veggie Beef soup in-house and Monica Pendleton of Crouse, NC makes and donates the Potato soup. Thanks to the RSP students and Hospice volunteers who donate the delicious desserts and hours of their time. 75% of the gross proceeds benefit Hospice Palliative Care of Lincoln County.

Raku Classes & Firings
Kilnfolk partners with Kadence Raku to bring our community opportunities to experience the magic of Raku! Learn about the process, join a class, or sign up for a future firing below.
What is Raku?
Not familiar with Raku? Here's a quick run down:   
Raku is an exciting, experimental, and unpredictable firing process that creates one-of-a-kind ceramic pieces. What makes it so special (and addicting!):
 Pottery is glazed with special Raku glazes, then placed in a kiln
 Pieces are removed from the kiln while glowing red hot
 The hot pottery is then placed in containers with combustible materials (sawdust, horse hair, newspaper, straw, leaves, etc.)
 These materials burn and create an environment where smoke interacts with the glazes
 The process creates unpredictable effects and patterns, often with crackled textures and shine
 Pieces are removed from the soot, then washed in water
 The final result is a stunning one-of-a-kind piece unlike any other!
This very collaborative process builds community as everyone gets involved in the firing. It's most successful as a group activity!
Through our partnership with Kadence Raku, we offer quarterly clay classes and Raku firings. Find our upcoming sessions below!
Nothing to book right now. Check back soon.
Raku FAQs
Who can join a Raku firing? Do I have to have experience?
If you're new to Raku, we recommend taking our Raku hand building class, which is held a couple of weeks before the firing event. During this class, you will create a piece using special Raku clay which can withstand the extreme temperature changes that occur during the glaze firing process.   
If you're a community potter or a member at Kilnfolk, or a multi-week student at Kilnfolk, you're welcome to join in as well and bring your own pieces. We have a separate option to book a spot in just the firing event for $30. Please be aware the piece you bring MUST be created with Raku clay, and already bisque fired.
What types of pieces can I make?
If you're joining one of our hand building classes prior to the firing, you will have the choice of some simple projects- sculpted animals, vases, other vessels, etc. Our instructor will guide you through basic hand building techniques, then you'll create a piece using those techniques.  
If you are a community potter, studio member, or multi-week student, your piece can be hand-built or wheel thrown as long as you're using Raku clay.
Where does the class and Raku firing take place?
The Raku hand building class takes place at Kilnfolk Clay Studio in downtown Vancouver, WA. The firing will take place at Kadence Collective in downtown Vancouver.
When can I take my piece home?
If you've created a piece during our hand building class, we will take care of the bisque firing, then we will bring your piece to the Raku firing event. Since the nature of Raku glaze firing is relatively instantaneous, you'll be able to take home your finished piece the same night of the firing.
Is there a minimum age requirement?
These events are for ages 18 and older.
"Raku is like a return to the basic elements, only with a heavy dose of unpredictability."

Meet The Cedar Oak Farm Pottery Instructors
Josh Barnes
Michelle Houchins
Josh and Michelle both have a gift for teaching, though they bring completely different artistic approaches to the studio.
Josh enjoys alternative firing techniques and embraces the "perfectly imperfect," creating an environment where creativity flows and results often exceed expectations.
Michelle is known as the resident "good luck charm," frequently helping others overcome challenges both in and outside of class. Her strengths lie in surface design, symmetry, and meticulous attention to detail.

Tanya Pohlmann
I earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts in ceramics and sculpture from Colorado State University, where great teachers helped me grow. They showed me to look deeper and the difference between making and creating. I enjoy the process and love creating unique pieces. I then got a master's in fine arts from the University of Hartford, where I learned to think creatively and explore art's meaning in my life. After graduation, I spent many years in corporate America but kept working with clay. That experience gave me the skills to start my own business.
I am excited to provide a different kind of environment for people to be creative. The Art School offers wheel throwing, Hand-Building and Sculpture classes.  In time, I hope to provide space for studio artist and start a regenerative educational garden with space for artists and gardening enthusiasts to enjoy.

What You'll Learn
We'll begin with an introduction to Raku firing, covering:
 How different glazes and firing techniques create unique surface effects
 Choosing the best glaze for your pieces
 Preparing your work for the kiln
 Raku safety and firing procedures
Throughout the workshop, you'll participate in every step of the firing process:
 Glazing your pottery
 Loading and firing the kiln
 Removing glowing red-hot pots from the kiln
 Placing work into reduction chambers filled with combustible materials
 Cleaning and revealing your finished pieces
One of the most exciting aspects of Raku is its immediacy. In just a few hours, you'll take your pottery from glazed bisque ware to finished work with beautiful, unpredictable results.

 Cotton or other natural-fiber clothing (no synthetic fabrics)
 Long sleeves

 Closed-toe shoes

Puppers Grove Pottery
Fine art ceramics. Raku fired North Carolina Pottery.
Puppers Grove Pottery is an independent ceramic studio devoted to handmade, non-functional work shaped by clay, smoke, flame, and time.
Built on our 12-acre homestead from the ground up
A studio grounded in fine art ceramics
Puppers Grove Pottery is centered on fine art ceramics rather than production ware.
The work begins with form, surface, and atmosphere – along with the tension between discipline and unpredictability that makes fired clay such a compelling medium. Each piece is created by hand as an individual work, shaped slowly and brought to completion through processes that leave their own distinct record.
These are ceramics intended not simply to serve a function, but to hold presence: pieces to live with, return to, and experience over time.

Why “Puppers Grove”
The name is not accidental. It’s rooted in the grove, in the life being built here, and in the dogs who have appointed themselves stewards of the place. One inspired the name; both remain deeply committed to oversight, morale, and occasional interference. The work is serious. The household remains less so.
Raku At The Center Of The Practice
Raku is a process that resists repetition. Flame, smoke, reduction, heat, and timing all leave their mark, producing surfaces shaped by crackle, carbon, luster, texture, and depth. The outcome can be guided, but never entirely controlled. That uncertainty is part of its expressive power.
Offered through limited collections and individual releases
One-of-a-kind work, released with intention
These pieces may take the form of vessels and sculptural ceramics, but they are created first and foremost as art objects, works defined by presence, surface, and the visible effects of fire. The emphasis remains on singularity rather than sameness, and on a slower process that allows each piece to arrive on its own terms. There will be no mass production here. The kiln would object, and the dogs have yet to approve any such nonsense.

Surface, fire, and process at the center of the work
Raku & Alternative Firing Methods
Puppers Grove Pottery is built around firing methods that emphasize variation, surface and the direct interaction between material and process.
Raku firing is central to the studio’s work. Flame, smoke, oxygen and timing all contribute to the final surface finish. While the process can be guided through experience, it cannot be fully controlled. Each firing introduces variables that leave a permanent record on the surface of the piece.
In addition to raku, the studio will explore alternative firing methods that expand on these ideas focusing on atmosphere, surface development and the relationship between heat and material. These processes are not used to produce uniform results. They are used to create work that reflects the conditions of its making, pieces shaped as much by fire and environment as by the hand.
Studio development is currently underway
Building a working ceramic studio from the ground up
Puppers Grove is being built deliberately, from the land up. What is taking shape is more than a workspace. It is a studio life organized around slower rhythms, sustained attention, and the long return to clay after years spent elsewhere. After nearly 30 years in a career that took me away from the studio, I am returning to a long-held focus: ceramic arts. This studio is being built from the ground up on our 12-acre homestead as Puppers Grove Pottery begins to take shape.
In the months ahead, we’ll share glimpses of the process – from raising the studio building, to the first firings, the first collection, and the life around it, the gradual shaping of a practice rooted in both discipline and place.  
There is still much to build. That, too, is part of the story.

raku or wood firing pottery studio Ralei.snippet:
Natalie Boorman
Natalie Boorman
Pit Fired and Raku Pottery
Raku Fired Pottery
THE RAKU FIRING PROCESS
Raku is a variation of smoke or atmospheric ceramic firing. Raku firing is an ancient method and there are many variations, Natalie’s way is to place a bisque fired vessel in a gas fired kiln. Depending on the type of glaze, she raises the kiln temperature rather quickly to desired heat, (about 1500 degrees for naked raku ), when she sees the glaze has matured, she quickly removes the vessel, using tongs, to a shallow hole in the ground, covers it with combustible material such as newspaper, wood chips, or hay and then tightly covers it with a tin lid. She uncovers it a few minutes later and sprays cold water on it. See Natalie’s Raku Pottery.

Raku Experience
This workshop provides a wonderful opportunity for a hands-on taster experience with Raku firing.
Raku is an exciting and instinctive rapid firing process, an ancient Japanese style of pottery where ceramic vessels are rapidly fired to 1000◦C. Taken from the kiln glowing red hot the pots are placed into organic matter and starved of oxygen to create vibrant colours and surface effects within the glaze and clay.
In the mid-20th century the process was modernised and moved away from traditional wood fired kilns to gas fired kilns. This is a highly unpredictable process which is always enthralling and filled with fun.
With a mixture of nervous excitement and thrilling anticipation the rewards can be great, producing spectacular and unique results with every piece. It is impossible for even a seasoned Raku potter to predict a result or be a perfectionist!
Cellan will guide you through the process of glazing and Raku firing up to 3 pieces. Students of all abilities from complete beginners to experienced potters are very welcome!
Each firing can take up to an hour, depending hugely on the weather conditions, affected by wind, humidity and temperature. The risk of thermal shock adds to the intensity, this means that pieces need to be carefully thought through, walls must not be too thin and joints can add points of weakness. Flat items such as trinket dishes or tiles are notorious for cracking and best avoided!
Using glazes, resists and oxides can give further interest to a finished vessel. Burnishing and carbonising non-coloured areas adds contrast and texture.
The risks, anticipation and thrill of removing glowing pieces from the kiln adds to the extraordinary excitement surrounding this technique!
